messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Environmental Scientist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs, Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

Vignette:
Miriam Calloway is a 77-year-old environmental scientist, single, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 73 following a rape that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. She had spent the evening at a professional conference dinner — one of the regional environmental summits she had attended annually for decades — and accepted a ride home from a male colleague she had known, or believed she had known, for several years. What happened in the car, and then in the parking structure outside her apartment building, dismantled assumptions she had carried for a lifetime about professional trust, about her own judgment, and about the safety of ordinary courtesies. The assault was prolonged. At one point he placed his hand on the back of her neck in what began as something that might have resembled an affectionate gesture before it became something else entirely. She did not scream. She had come to believe, in the months that followed, that her failure to scream was the reason it had happened at all.

In the weeks after the assault, Miriam continued to go into work at the environmental consulting firm where she has spent the last eleven years of her career. Her work requires periodic site visits to open parcels of land — wetlands assessments, soil sampling, habitat surveys — and it was during one of these early visits, standing alone in a wide, flat meadow with no tree line nearby and no clear path back to her vehicle, that she first felt what she now recognises as a kind of paralysis. The exposure of it — the openness, the absence of walls or corners — registered as danger in a way she could not reason herself out of. She began to find reasons to send junior colleagues in her place. Over the following months, her field visits dropped from several per week to almost none, and her supervisor has begun asking questions she does not know how to answer.

Inside the office, Miriam has reorganised her habits around a logic that feels, to her, entirely rational. Before entering any room she identifies where the exits are. She sits with her back to the wall. When a male colleague rounds a corner quickly or reaches past her for something on a shelf, her body responds before her mind can intervene — a sharp intake of breath, a step backward, hands rising slightly. She avoids being alone in the office with any man, scheduling her arrival and departure to coincide with the presence of female staff, and she has declined two after-hours project meetings on grounds she described to colleagues as scheduling conflicts. She no longer makes eye contact easily, particularly with men, having come to understand eye contact as an invitation she is no longer willing to extend.

At home, evenings are structured around listening. She tracks the sounds of her building — the elevator, footsteps in the hallway, the particular sound of someone testing a door handle — and cannot settle until she has confirmed, repeatedly, that each sound has an innocent explanation. Sleep is fitful and short. She has stopped attending the neighbourhood walking group she joined three years ago, and a close friend who reached out to embrace her at a birthday gathering last spring was met with a flinch that neither of them has directly addressed since. Miriam has come to believe that warmth and physical affection are vectors for something she cannot afford to be wrong about again. She rehearses, regularly, the sequence of choices she made the night of the assault — the dinner, the conversation, the acceptance of the ride — and turns them over looking for the precise moment her behaviour made what followed possible. She has not found it, but she has not stopped looking.

What finally brought Miriam to seek help was a conversation with her physician during a routine appointment, in which she disclosed, for the first time and with considerable difficulty, what had happened. Her physician referred her directly. Miriam arrived at the intake appointment having written notes beforehand, because she was afraid she would not be able to speak. What she most fears is that the shame she carries — for what was done to her body, for what she believes she invited — is something a therapist will confirm rather than challenge. What she most hopes, though she expressed this only obliquely, is that she might one day walk into an open field and feel nothing more than the wind.
